notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0555.tlg001.perseus-: The text is marked corrupt (†) at 'of Apollo' in the list of oracles; the name there is doubtful.
'Nourished for matter' renders the obscure εἰς ὕλας τρεφομένη (perhaps 'fattened as fuel'). 'Toothless' (νωδοί) is an odd word for moles and may conceal another reading.

nodes.text: Do not, then, busy yourselves with godless sanctuaries, nor with the mouths of chasms full of marvel-mongering, nor with the Thesprotian cauldron or the Cirrhaean tripod or the Dodonaean bronze; and the old tree honoured in the desert sands, and the oracle there, withered along with the oak itself, leave them to myths grown old. The spring of Castalia, at any rate, has been silenced, and that other spring, of Colophon; and the other prophetic streams are likewise dead, and, emptied at last of their vanity, they have been shown up, late but shown up all the same, as having run dry together with their own myths. Tell us too of the useless oracles of that other divination, or rather madness: the Clarian, the Pythian, the Didymaean, that of Amphiaraus, † of Apollo, of Amphilochus; and, if you will, dedicate along with them the portent-watchers and the bird-watchers and the interpreters of dreams; and bring and set beside the Pythian, all together, the flour-diviners and the barley-diviners and the ventriloquists who are still honoured among the many. Yes, and let the sanctuaries of the Egyptians and the oracles of the dead of the Etruscans be handed over to darkness. Truly mad are these schools of sophistry of faithless men, these gambling-dens of undiluted error; and partners in the trade of this sorcery are goats trained for divination, and ravens taught by men to give oracles to men.

Consider for a little, if you will, the divine kindness from the beginning. The first man, when he was in paradise, played freely, since he was a child of God; but when, falling under pleasure (the serpent is an allegory of pleasure crawling on its belly, an earthly vice, nourished for matter), he was led astray by desires, the child, coming to manhood through disobedience and refusing to listen to his father, was ashamed before God. Such was the power of pleasure: the man who through simplicity was free was found bound by sins. The Lord wished to free him again from his bonds, and, binding himself in flesh (this is a divine mystery), he subdued the serpent and enslaved the tyrant, death; and, most wonderful of all, that man who had been led astray by pleasure, who had been bound by corruption, he showed to be free, with hands outstretched. O mystic wonder! The Lord has been laid low, and man has risen up; and he who fell from paradise receives a greater prize for obedience: the heavens. Therefore it seems to me that, since the Word himself has come to us from heaven, we ought no longer to go to human teaching, busily searching out Athens and the rest of Greece, and Ionia besides. For if our teacher is he who filled all things with holy powers, with creation, salvation, beneficence, lawgiving, prophecy and teaching, then the teacher now instructs [us in] all things, and the whole world has already become Athens and Greece through the Word. For surely you will not have believed a poetic myth that records Minos the Cretan as the familiar companion of Zeus, and yet disbelieve us, who have become disciples of God and have taken up the wisdom that is truly real, which the foremost of philosophy only hinted at, but which the disciples of Christ have both grasped and proclaimed. And indeed the whole Christ, so to speak, is not divided: there is neither barbarian nor Jew nor Greek, not male, not female, but a new man, refashioned by the Holy Spirit of God. Then, the other counsels and precepts are meagre and concern particular matters: whether one should marry, whether take part in public life, whether have children; but the only universal exhortation, one that plainly bears on the whole of life, at every moment, in every circumstance, reaching toward the supreme end, life, is reverence for God; and according to it alone we must live, so that we may live forever. Philosophy, as the elders say, is a long-drawn-out counsel, wooing the eternal love of wisdom; but the commandment of the Lord shines far, enlightening the eyes. Receive Christ, receive sight, receive your light, so that you may know well both god and man. Desirable is the Word who has enlightened us, more than gold and precious stone; he is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. For how is he not desirable, who made clear the mind that had been buried in darkness and sharpened the light-bearing eyes of the soul? For just as, if there were no sun, all things would be night for all the other stars, so, if we had not known the Word and been illuminated by him, we would be no better than fowls being fattened, fattened in darkness and reared for death. Let us make room for the light, so that we may make room for God; let us make room for the light and become disciples of the Lord. This indeed is what he has promised the Father: I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise. Sing and declare to me God your Father: your declarations will save, your song will instruct me. Until now I wandered seeking God; but since you light my way, Lord, and I find God through you and receive the Father from you, I become your joint heir, since you were not ashamed of your brother. Let us take away, then, let us take away the forgetting of the truth; clearing away the ignorance and the darkness that stand in the way like a mist over the sight, let us behold the God who truly is, first raising to him this cry of praise: Hail, light! A light from heaven has shone forth upon us who were buried in darkness and shut up in the shadow of death, purer than the sun, sweeter than the life here. That light is eternal life, and whatever has shared in it lives; and night fears the light and, setting out of fear, gives way to the day of the Lord. All things have become sleepless light, and the setting has turned into a rising. This is what the new creation has meant; for the sun of righteousness, who rides over all things, ranges equally over humankind, imitating the Father, who makes his sun rise upon all men, and sprinkles down the dew of truth. He has changed the setting into a rising and crucified death into life; and snatching man out of destruction he has hung him up to the sky, transplanting corruption into incorruption and changing earth into heaven, he the husbandman of God, giving favourable signs, rousing the peoples to good work, reminding them of true livelihood, and granting us the Father's inheritance, truly great and divine and inalienable, making man divine by heavenly teaching, putting laws into their mind and writing them on [their] heart. What laws does he inscribe? That all shall know God, from small to great; and I will be merciful to them, says God, and I will not remember their sins. Let us receive the laws of life, let us obey God when he exhorts us, let us learn him, so that he may be merciful; let us pay him, though he needs nothing, a grateful wage for the good we enjoy, piety, as a kind of rent to God for our dwelling here. Gold for bronze, a hundred oxen's worth for nine. For a little faith he gives you this great earth to till, water to drink and other water to sail, air to breathe, fire to serve you, a world to live in; he has allowed you to send out a colony from here to the heavens; all these great works and gifts he has let out to you for a little faith. Then, those who have trusted in sorcerers accept amulets and incantations as supposedly bringing safety, and do you not wish to fasten on yourselves the heavenly one himself, the saving Word, and, trusting in the incantation of God, to be freed from passions, which are the diseases of the soul, and torn away from sin? For sin is eternal death. Truly, utterly toothless and blind like moles, you spend your lives in darkness doing nothing but eating, wasting away in corruption. But there is, there is the truth that has cried out: Out of darkness light shall shine. Let the light shine, then, in the hidden part of man, in the heart, and let the rays of knowledge rise, revealing and making shine forth the man hidden within, the disciple of the light, the friend and joint heir of Christ, especially when the most precious and most venerable name of a good father has come to the knowledge of a pious and good child, a father who commands gentle things and enjoins on his child what brings salvation. He who obeys him gains in every way: he follows God, he obeys the Father, he has come to know him while astray, he has loved God, he has loved his neighbour, he has fulfilled the commandment, he seeks the prize, he claims the promise. It is always God's purpose to save the flock of men. For this reason the good God sent the good shepherd; and the Word, unfolding the truth, showed men the height of salvation, so that they might either repent and be saved, or refuse to obey and be judged. This is the proclamation of righteousness: to those who obey, good news; to those who refuse to hear, a court of judgement. But the loud-clamouring trumpet, when it sounds, gathers soldiers and proclaims war; and shall not Christ, who has breathed a melody of peace to the ends of the earth, gather his own soldiers of peace? He has indeed gathered, O man, by blood and by the Word, his bloodless army, and has entrusted to them the kingdom of heaven. Christ's trumpet is his gospel: he has sounded it, and we have heard. Let us arm ourselves in peace, putting on the breastplate of righteousness and taking up the shield of faith and setting on the helmet of salvation; and let us sharpen the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. So the apostle draws us up in peaceful array. These are our invulnerable arms; armed with these, let us form our line against the evil one; let us quench the fiery darts of the evil one with the watery points tempered by the Word, repaying his good deeds with thankful blessings and honouring God with the divine Word. For while you are still speaking, it says, he will say: Here I am. O this holy and blessed power, through which God shares citizenship with men! It is better, then, and finer to become at once an imitator and a servant of the best of all beings; for no one will be able to imitate God except through the things by which he serves him in holiness, nor again to serve and revere him except by imitating him. The heavenly and truly divine love comes to men in this way, when somewhere in the soul itself the truly beautiful, rekindled by the divine Word, is able to shine forth; and, greatest of all, salvation runs together with the genuine wish to be saved, will and life being yoked together, so to speak. Therefore this exhortation of the truth alone is likened to the most faithful of friends, staying with us until our last breath, and proving, by the whole and perfect spirit of the soul, a good escort to those who depart for heaven. Why, then, do I exhort you? I am eager for you to be saved. This is what Christ wills; in a word, he grants you life. And who is he? Learn briefly: the Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who regenerates man and brings him back up to the truth; the goad of salvation; who drives out corruption, who chases away death; who has built a temple in men, so that he may establish God in men. Purify the temple; and leave pleasures and idleness, like a flower of a day, to wind and fire; but cultivate wisely the fruits of self-control, and set yourself up as a first-fruits offering to God, so that you may be not only the work but also the grace of God; and both befit the friend of Christ: to appear worthy of the kingdom, and to have been deemed worthy of the kingdom.
